bib.title: Survey on Factuality in Large Language Models: Knowledge, Retrieval and Domain-Specificity

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Survey on Factuality in Large Language Models: Knowledge, Retrieval and Domain-Specificity", Cunxiang Wang, Xiaoze Liu, Yuanhao Yue, + 15 others (corresponding: Yue Zhang, Westlake). Preprint: arXiv:2310.07521v3, 16 Dec 2023. The PDF is set in the ACM Computing Surveys template, but with unfilled placeholders ("Vol. 1, No. 1 ... December 2018", "© 2018", DOI "XXXXXXX.XXXXXXX"), so the PDF does not show acceptance there. Cite it as a preprint.

COVERAGE: 62 of 62 pages; 261,577 of 261,577 chars extracted. Pages 1-47 (body through Conclusion) were read in full. Pages 47-62 are the reference list (317 entries), which I skimmed only. There are no appendices and no limitations section.

DOES IT CONTRIBUTE ANYTHING OF ITS OWN? Almost nothing empirical. It runs no experiments; every number is copied from the cited papers. Its own contributions are organisational:
- a definition of factuality
- the factuality versus hallucination 2x2 (Table 2)
- a four-way metric grouping (Table 3)
- an error-cause taxonomy at model, retrieval and inference level (Table 1, Sec 4.2)
- compiled benchmark tables (Tables 4-8)

CLAIMS

- claim: Factuality is defined as generating content that follows facts groundable to reliable sources.
  number: none
  setup: definitional; only undisputed facts whose truth can be determined
  quote: "By factuality in LLMs we refer to the capability of large language models for generating contents that follow factual information, which encompasses commonsense, world knowledge and domain facts. The factual information can be grounded to reliable sources, such as dictionaries, Wikipedia or textbooks"
  where: p4, Sec 2.2

- claim: Hallucination and factuality are separate axes. Hallucination is deviation from the source or prompt; factuality is agreement with world facts. An output can be either one without the other.
  number: none
  setup: definitional; Table 2 gives the four cells
  quote: "If the generated content contains accurate information but diverges from the prompt's specifics, it's a hallucination but not a factuality issue."
  where: p6. Table 2: "Hallucinated but Factual: 1. Outputs that are unfaithful to the prompt but remain factually correct"; "Non-Factual but Non-Hallucinated: 1. Outputs where the LLM states 'I don't know'... 2. Outputs that are partially correct". The hallucination definition is borrowed from Ji et al. and OpenAI: "produce content that is nonsensical or untruthful in relation to certain sources."

- claim: Faithfulness is not defined by the survey itself. It appears only as "unfaithful to the prompt" inside the hallucination cell, and in the RAGAS summary.
  number: none
  setup: RAGAS, as described by the survey
  quote: "the faithfulness score being the ratio of faithful assertions to the total number of assertions"
  where: p20

- claim: The metric taxonomy has four groups (Table 3).
  number: none
  setup: (1) Rule-based: Exact Match, Accuracy/P/R/F, Calibration, Brier, MC1/MC2, BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, QUIP-Score. (2) Neural: ADEM, BERTScore, BLEURT, BARTScore. (3) Human: AIS/Auto-AIS, FActScore. (4) LLM-based: GPTScore, GPT-judge, truth*info, LLM-Eval.
  quote: "(1) Rule-based evaluation metrics; (2) Neural evaluation metrics; (3) Human evaluation metrics; and (4) LLM-based evaluation metrics."
  where: p8-12

- claim: FActScore scores the percentage of atomic facts supported by a knowledge source.
  number: 42% to 71%
  setup: human evaluation of biographies from InstructGPT, ChatGPT and PerplexityAI; precision falls as entities get rarer
  quote: "with FActScores ranging from 42% to 71%"
  where: p12

- claim: LLM-as-judge for correctness has reported negative results.
  number: none
  setup: Wang et al. [263] on NQ/TriviaQA with GPT-3.5 as grader; Fu et al. [70] on summary factuality
  quote: "they evaluate whether the GPT-3.5 can assess the correctness of LLM-generated responses, and find negative results, even if the golden answer is also presented"
  where: p19. Same page: "find no significant correlation between LLM's factuality indicators and human evaluations".

- claim: Benchmark table (Table 4) gives representative scores for 14 benchmarks.
  number: MMLU GPT-4 86.4; ALCE citation precision GPT-3.5 73.9 vs LLaMA-33B 23.0; FreshQA GPT-4 28.6
  setup: MMLU is 5-shot accuracy; ALCE is ASQA with 3 passages; FreshQA is strict accuracy with a null prompt. All are 2023-era models, copied from the source papers.
  quote: "GPT-4: 86.4 GPT-3.5: 70 LLaMA2-70B: 68.9"; "(ASQA, 3-psg, citation prec) GPT-3.5: 73.9 LLaMA-33B: 23.0"; "(strict ACC, null prompt) GPT-4: 28.6 GPT-3.5: 26.0"
  where: p14. The full list: MMLU, TruthfulQA, C-Eval, AGIEval, HaluEval, BigBench, ALCE, QUIP, PopQA, UniLC, Pinocchio, SelfAware, RealTimeQA, FreshQA.

- claim: Retrieval-level error causes are insufficient information, distracting information, unrecognised misinformation, and misinterpretation.
  number: 14% vs 6%; 23%
  setup: ReAct's error analysis on fact-checking/QA, as reported by the survey
  quote: "while CoT has 14% of its correct answers containing incorrect reasoning steps or facts, ReAct only has 6%... However, ReAct have 23% of its errors resulting from search errors."
  where: p28 (taxonomy), p36 (numbers). Table 1 on p5 has worked examples: answers that follow the retrieved context yet are wrong (the Citizen Mavzik director, the conflicting James Vincent documents). These bear directly on "faithful is not correct".

- claim: Under knowledge conflict, FiD rarely falls back on memorised answers.
  number: less than 3.6%
  setup: FiD on NQ, from [24]
  quote: "FiD models rarely resort to memorization (less than 3.6% for NQ) compared to RAG models"
  where: p26

LIMITS
- No original experiments and no meta-analysis.
- The authors concede that the enhancement table is not comparable across rows: "performance metrics for different methods, even when evaluating the same metric on the same dataset, may not be directly comparable" (p29).
- Summarisation faithfulness is deliberately excluded (p7), so the NLI/QA-based consistency literature (FactCC, QAGS, SummaC) is absent.
- No formal definition of faithfulness or grounding tiers. Retrieval metrics (recall@k, MRR, nDCG) are not covered.
- The taxonomy is loose. FActScore is filed under "Human" although it has an automated variant. BLEU/ROUGE are described as measuring "factual consistency" without critique. Table 5's "token-level versus sentence-level" granularity is never explained.
- Dated: models are GPT-3.5/GPT-4/LLaMA-2 and literature runs to late 2023.

BUILDS ON
- Hallucination definition: Ji et al. [111] and OpenAI [193].
- Attribution: AIS, Rashkin et al. [215]; Auto-AIS, Gao et al. [76].
- Min et al. FActScore [180]; Lin et al. TruthfulQA [147]; Es et al. RAGAS [61]; Manakul et al. SelfCheckGPT [168]; Gao et al. ALCE [77].
- It positions itself against the hallucination surveys [103, 216, 291, 309]. I did not verify the reference years individually.

CODE: none.

FIGURES: at most one candidate. Table 2 (p6, "Comparison between the factuality issue and the hallucination issue") is a table, not a figure, but it is the fastest way to show the faithful-versus-correct 2x2. Of the two real figures, Fig. 1 (p3, taxonomy tree) is a section map only, and Fig. 2 (p29) covers enhancement methods; neither suits this note.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Extraction is clean, but table cells are linearised, so the row/column alignment in Tables 4-9 was reconstructed from order.
- Source inconsistencies:
  - Table 4 cites AGIEval as [105], which is the C-Eval reference; the bibliography has it as [313].
  - SelfAware GPT-4 F1 is 75.47 in Table 4 and "75.5" in the text.
  - Sec 3.1.2 says "three prominent metrics" and then lists four.
  - The template dates (2018) are placeholders.
- The numbers above are second-hand, as the survey reports them. I did not check them against the original papers.
